thread.title: Reed helps secure money to test seawater at beaches statewide
thread.title_full: Reed helps secure money to test seawater at beaches statewide

author: ohtadmin
title: Reed helps secure money to test seawater at beaches statewide
text:
Rhode Island is getting financial aid to monitor the water quality of Narragansett Bay following a 2025 season that had 123 closures of beaches due to the concentration of enterococci bacteria.
U.S. Sen. Jack Reed, a Jamestown resident, helped secure $210,000 from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency through the Beaches Environmental Assessment and Coastal Health Act.
The money will be used by the Rhode Island Department of Health to collect and study samples of seawater at the Ocean State’s most popular beaches, including Mackerel Cove.
“Safe, clean beaches are important to Rhode Islanders and our communities,” Reed said. “A day at the beach to be safe, fun and healthy. … Forget sharks. The greatest risk to swimmers’ health is tiny, microscopic bacteria. That is why it is so important to be proactive.”
Reed rescued the grants from the Trump administration’s chopping block, which led to $9.75 million in aid nationwide in 2026.
Swimming in contaminated waters can cause gastrointestinal illnesses, skin rashes, sore throats, ear infections, eye infections and fever. Reed called President Donald Trump’s attempt to eliminate the money “a short-sighted effort” that would put families at risk.
Rhode Island has more than 400 miles of coastline and the program oversees testing at about 60 beaches. Closures may be caused by contamination due to heavy rainfall that creates urban runoff and sewage overflows.
If the concentration of enterococci bacteria exceeds 60 colony-forming units per 100 milliliters, a temporary closure is issued until the quality improves.
Easton’s Beach is the only site so far to be closed in 2026. It reopened June 1 after being closed for three days.
The last time Mackerel Cove was closed for swimming was June 2021. The water quality returned to an acceptable level 36 hours later and the beach reopened.
Prior to that, Mackerel Cove had not been closed to swimming since June 2016 for surpassing the threshold. There also was a closure in 2008.
Beyond the adverse health effects from contaminated water, closed beaches also signal economic warnings to policymakers, Reed said. Address the environmental issues or deal with the outflow of tourism and recreational dollars.
“New England’s beaches are central to the region’s coastal way of life, sustaining communities and driving local economies,” said Mark Sanborn, New England’s administrator for the EPA. “This funding helps protect human health by ensuring beaches are regularly monitored so Americans can enjoy clean, safe water for swimming and recreation.”
